thread.title: Apple and other tech companies sound the alarm on Trump's China tariff plans

author: morningstar.com
title: Apple and other tech companies sound the alarm on Trump's China tariff plans
text:
By Therese Poletti, MarketWatch
Proposed tariffs on $200 billion in Chinese imports would hurt consumers and America while potentially helping China, companies say
Apple Inc. isn't the only company concerned that President Donald Trump's latest proposed tariffs on an additional $200 billion of goods made in China will lead to higher prices for consumers, lower profits for the tech industry and slower economic growth.
Hundreds of U.S. companies, including a swath of tech companies, are concerned about the potential impact on prices, profits, and in the case of many smaller companies and startups, their viability. Companies, industry groups and analysts are also concerned that the next round of possible tariffs -- possibly as high as 25% -- will hurt the competitive stance of U.S. tech companies, affect their ability to continue to invest in research on future products, and could lead to a recession in one of the hot growth engines in technology -- the semiconductor industry.
Read MarketWatch's trade-war tracker here (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trade-war-tracker-here-are-the-new-levies-imposed-and-threatened-2018-06-22)
Apple (AAPL) drew attention to the issue late Friday, with its letter to U.S. Trade Representative Robert Lighthizer, that said the proposed tariffs will impact its prices (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-says-proposed-tariffs-would-hit-the-apple-watch-airpods-mac-mini-and-other-products-2018-09-07)on the Apple Watch, Apple AirPods, the MacMini, cables, chargers and other products. That was just one of thousands of letters submitted as public comments, however, and more than 300 companies testified (https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/enforcement/301Investigations/Section%20301%20Tariffs%20Hearing%20Panel%20Schedule.pdf) at Capitol Hill hearings in August (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-says-proposed-tariffs-would-hit-the-apple-watch-airpods-mac-mini-and-other-products-2018-09-07)-- so many that the hearings had to be extended to six days to accommodate more testimony.
Among the U.S. tech companies or associations that testified were the Semiconductor Industry Association; SEMI, the semiconductor equipment association; the Consumer Technology Association, which runs the annual CES trade show; iRobot Corp. (IRBT); Logitech (LOGI) ; and Fitbit Inc.(FIT) .
"With the two prior tariff lists, already in effect, the administration was able to avoid creating any significant impact on consumers," Greg R. Pearsonan, an Intel Corp. (INTC) senior vice president and global policy officer, said in a letter the chip giant submitted Thursday. "The proposed List 3 is a game changer for the American consumer -- especially if the tariffs are increased from 10% to 25%."
The list of products affected by the proposed tariffs (https://ustr.gov/sites/default/files/301/2018-0026%20China%20FRN%207-10-2018_0.pdf)includes a section on electronics that begins with "machines for the reception, conversion and transmission or regeneration of voice, images or other data, including switching and routing apparatus," and includes "printed circuit assemblies" and "semiconductor media."
Many companies and industry associations pointed out in their letters or testimony that U.S. companies are paying tariffs on products of their own design, which are being manufactured or, in some cases, assembled in China, and then shipped back to the U.S. for final assembly and export. The Information Technology Industry Council noted that this could also have an impact on U.S. jobs, if that supply chain is disrupted.
"Companies may be forced to downsize their production in the U.S. and manufacturing facilities or move overseas," Naomi Wilson, director for China and greater Asia at the ITIC, said in her testimony.
Don't miss: The current tech bubble is a Chinese import (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/the-current-tech-bubble-is-a-chinese-import-2018-09-06)
The Consumer Technology Association said it identified 380 codes from the list which would "cause significant harm" to its industry, its member companies, as well as consumers.
"Of concern are items that allow Americans to access the internet, such as servers, desktop computers, printed circuit assemblies and connected devices," said Sage Chandler, vice president for international trade at the CTA, in her testimony in August.
The CTA did a study on some of the possible impacts (https://prod1.cta.tech/CTA/media/policyImages/Estimated-Impacts-of-Proposed-Tariffs-on-Imports-from-China_-Printed-Circuit-Assemblies-and-Wireless-Telecommunications-Accessories.pdf), cautioning that the tariffs on printed circuit board assemblies and connected devices will cause price increases of up to 6%, impacting even products made entirely with U.S. labor and components.
"Those price increases are expected to reduce consumer purchasing by 12%," the CTA said in a statement (https://www.cta.tech/News/Press-Releases/2018/September/$200-Billion-Tariffs-Vulnerable-to-Legal-Challenge.aspx), adding that it estimates the tariffs on connected devices alone are expected to cost American shoppers an additional $3.2 billion annually.
Dan Hutcheson, president of VLSI Research Inc. in San Jose, said the tariffs already enacted against the auto industry have had an impact on semiconductors being sold to car makers, one of the hottest segments in the chip business.
"The car manufacturers started slowing down their purchases of chips because they don't know what's going to happen to the car market," he said.
"There is a whole global supply chain in which the chips cross oceans multiple times," Hutcheson said. "They [companies] could possibly pay tariffs multiple times. Kind of like if you walk out of Disneyland and don't get stamped and have to walk back in and pay again."
Fitbit, which agreed with other companies that the tariffs would hurt its business because it would have to raise prices, also noted that the tariffs could give Chinese wearables rivals a leg up in the U.S. market and could even pose a national security threat.
Opinion: Now would be the time for Apple to buy Tesla, and kick Elon Musk out of the driver's seat (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/now-would-be-the-time-for-apple-to-buy-tesla-and-kick-musk-out-of-the-drivers-seat-2018-08-27)
"The proposed tariffs would make wearables costlier and, in many cases, inaccessible to consumers, making less expensive offerings from Chinese competitors more attractive and allowing them to gain market share," said Andy Missan, Fitbit general counsel, in his testimony last week. Chinese giants Huawei and Xiaomi Corp. (1810.HK) have gained two of the top four spots in global market for wearable devices, he noted.
"While Fitbit stores its sensitive data solely on its U.S. servers subject to strict privacy and security safeguards, there is very little preventing the same data collected by Chinese companies from ending up on Chinese servers, accessible on demand by the Chinese government raising serious privacy and national security concerns," Missan added. "Do we really want this sensitive health, location and financial data of Americans to be stored on Chinese servers?"
On Monday, UBS Securities economist Seth Carpenter said in a note to clients that the U.S. Global Domestic Product growth is going to slow further as a result of the latest tariffs. "The tariffs cause fourth quarter GDP growth to slow to a 1.5% annualized pace. In our baseline forecast growth snaps back to around 3 percent in the first quarter of 2019. 25% tariffs would cause a larger slowdown in GDP that could continue into the first part of next year."
See also: Apple is worth $1 trillion because of Tim Cook (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/apple-is-worth-1-trillion-because-of-tim-cook-2018-08-05)
Trump has spent a lot of time bragging about GDP growth (http://www.marketwatch.com/story/trump-today-president-makes-false-claim-about-gdp-and-unemployment-2018-09-10) during his tenure. But the tariffs on Chinese goods, and in particular the latest proposal which really targets electronics, is going to seriously mar one of the big stars in the U.S. -- the tech business.
Hutcheson believes that the tariffs will lead to the first semiconductor downturn since 2012, and possibly worse.
"It probably will cause a recession in the semi industry," he said. "We have had some really good years here, so you could argue that we are due for a slowdown."
Hutcheson also noted that the industry is gearing up for the big second half of the year and the all-important holiday season for consumer electronics.
"We are coming into a very critical time. If all of a sudden electronics coming over from China are marked up, the electronics industry is going to be killed," he said.
-Therese Poletti;
